In the gap straight down between two roofs, a narrow court with one lit basement window and a barrow of oranges left standing at the bottom of it.
Fog has filled every street right up to the first-floor windows, so the roofs and the towers stand out of it like islands and the packed luminous fog itself is what fills the gap.
A canal runs through the gap with a laden barge crossing it, the barge's funnel smoke coming straight up past the leads and in among the cables.
The gaslamps have just been lit all the way down a street in the gap — a row of small warm points going away under the smoke, each with its own puddle of light.
A foundry yard in the gap is throwing up a hot orange bloom that lights the whole undersides of the cables above it and the bellies of the chimney pots.
An elevated tram is crossing the gap on a riveted viaduct, sparks under its wheels and its open upper deck full of passengers all facing the same way.
A great stone railway viaduct strides across the gap on tall arches and a goods train is going over it slowly, its steam rolling down between the buildings.
In the gap below, a glass-roofed courtyard full of potted palms with two figures the size of seeds crossing it.
A market has set up in the gap — forty striped canvas awnings packed edge to edge, with a wedge of lamplight coming up between two of them.
The gap below is all water: a flooded street with a rowing boat in it and reflections of the lit windows going down and down.
A brewery yard in the gap with a dray horse standing patient between the shafts and barrels stacked in a pyramid beside it.
In the gap, a builder's scaffold of lashed poles climbs the whole face of a gutted house, with a hoist wheel at its top and a man leaning on it.
A steep flight of public stairs zigzags down through the gap between the buildings, lit by one lamp at each landing, with a dog coming up it.
The gap holds a small green graveyard with three plane trees in it, absurdly quiet, one bench and a cat on the bench.
A tangle of washing ropes crosses the gap at three heights, loaded with sheets, and the sheets are all blowing the same direction like signals of their own.
In the gap, an ironmonger's yard piled with scrap — a hill of rusted iron with a boy standing on top of it holding something up.
A cab rank fills the gap below, six hansoms nose to tail with their lamps lit and the horses' breath showing.
The gap is spanned low down by a covered wooden bridge between two upper floors, its little windows lit, someone crossing inside it.
In the gap, a canal lock is filling: the water boiling white at the gates and a narrowboat rising slowly in the chamber.
A theatre's back alley fills the gap, stacked with rolled canvas and a painted cut-out tree leaned against the brick, and a stage doorway blazing warm light into the dark.
The gap below holds a knot of five streets meeting at once, a stone obelisk in the middle of them and traffic wheeling round it.
A glasshouse roof glows faintly green down in the gap, deep inside a walled garden that nobody up here can get to.
In the gap, a fire brigade has its ladder up against a smoking window, the horses still in harness and a knot of onlookers standing well back along the wall.
A bathhouse chimney down in the gap is pumping a fat white plume of steam straight up, and the steam is going right through the lower cables.
The gap is filled with the vast dark shape of a dry dock, a ship's iron hull in it propped on timbers, men no bigger than pins on the timbers beneath it.
